blocks.text: Safety evaluation checks whether a fine-tuned model produces harmful, biased, or otherwise unsafe outputs, a distinct evaluation dimension from the quality and hallucination metrics covered elsewhere in this module, since a response can be fluent, accurate, and still genuinely unsafe.

This topic covers the categories of unsafe behavior safety evaluation targets, how red teaming works as a testing methodology, and the tradeoff between blocking harmful requests and over-refusing benign ones.
1. Safety as a Distinct Evaluation Dimension

blocks.alt: Quality evaluation is compared against safety evaluation

blocks.text: Quality metrics covered earlier in this module, BLEU, ROUGE, human evaluation, all measure how good a response is at its intended task, safety evaluation instead asks a different question entirely, whether the response could cause harm, a model can score well on quality while still failing safety evaluation badly.
2. Categories of Unsafe Behavior

blocks.alt: Harmful content generation, biased output, and jailbreak success are all unsafe behaviors

blocks.text: Safety evaluation typically covers several distinct categories, generating genuinely harmful content, producing outputs that reflect unfair bias against particular groups, and being successfully manipulated by adversarial prompts, jailbreaks, into ignoring its intended safety behavior.

blocks.text: 3. Testing With Adversarial Prompts

blocks.alt: An adversarial prompt is run against the model under test, producing a safe or unsafe response

blocks.text: Safety evaluation deliberately includes adversarial prompts, questions crafted specifically to try to elicit unsafe behavior, testing not just how a model behaves on typical benign inputs but how robust its safety behavior is under deliberate pressure.
4. Red Teaming as a Methodology

blocks.alt: A red team prompt set is run against the model, flagging unsafe outputs

blocks.text: Red teaming means having a dedicated team, sometimes human experts, sometimes another model, deliberately try to find inputs that make the model behave unsafely, systematically probing for weaknesses before real users, malicious or otherwise, might find them in production.

blocks.title: Red teaming is adversarial by design
blocks.content: Effective red teaming assumes the perspective of someone actively trying to break the model safety behavior, a genuinely different mindset from typical quality-focused evaluation covered elsewhere in this module.

blocks.text: 5. Refusal Rate vs Over-Refusal Rate

blocks.alt: Refusal rate is compared against over refusal rate

blocks.text: Refusal rate measures how often a model correctly declines genuinely unsafe requests, over-refusal rate measures how often it incorrectly declines benign requests that merely resemble unsafe ones, both matter, a model that refuses everything technically has a perfect refusal rate but is nearly useless.
6. Measuring Bias Across Groups

blocks.alt: Model outputs are compared across demographic group A and demographic group B

blocks.text: Bias evaluation typically compares model outputs across matched prompts that differ only in a demographic detail, name, gender, or group reference, checking whether the model treats otherwise identical requests differently in a way that reflects unfair bias rather than a legitimate distinction.

blocks.text: 7. Automated Safety Classifiers

blocks.alt: A safety classifier model scores each response

blocks.text: Running every response through a dedicated safety classifier model, trained specifically to detect harmful content, is a common way to scale safety evaluation across a large number of test prompts, similar in spirit to the automated fact-checking models covered in the hallucination evaluation topic, though safety classifiers still benefit from periodic human spot-checking.
8. Safety Evaluation Throughout Fine-Tuning

Safety behavior can shift meaningfully during fine-tuning, sometimes a narrow task-focused fine-tuning run inadvertently weakens a base model existing safety training, tracking safety evaluation metrics across checkpoints, not just at the very end, helps catch this kind of regression before deployment.
9. Balancing Safety With Usefulness

The practical goal is not maximizing refusal rate in isolation, but finding the point where genuinely unsafe requests are reliably declined while benign requests, even ones that superficially resemble unsafe ones, are still handled helpfully, a balance that requires both refusal rate and over-refusal rate to be tracked together.
Worked Example

A team fine-tunes a customer support model and runs it through a red team prompt set covering harmful content requests, bias probes across demographic name pairs, and known jailbreak patterns from published research.

The evaluation reveals the fine-tuned model has a slightly higher over-refusal rate than the base model, declining some entirely benign troubleshooting questions that happen to mention words associated with the fine-tuning task narrow safety filtering, prompting the team to adjust their fine-tuning data to better distinguish genuinely unsafe requests from superficially similar benign ones.
Common Mistakes

items: Evaluating only refusal rate on unsafe prompts while ignoring over-refusal on benign ones
Assuming a model that scores well on quality metrics must also be safe, when the two dimensions are independent
Running safety evaluation only once before deployment instead of tracking it across fine-tuning checkpoints
Relying entirely on an automated safety classifier without any human review of ambiguous or borderline cases

blocks.text: Practice

Write three prompts, one clearly unsafe, one clearly benign, and one benign but superficially resembling the unsafe one, then reason through what refusal behavior you would want a well calibrated model to show for each, and why the third case is the hardest to get right.
Key Takeaway

Safety evaluation checks for harmful content, bias, and jailbreak vulnerability using adversarial and red team testing, a dimension entirely separate from quality or hallucination evaluation covered earlier in this module, and effective safety evaluation always weighs refusal rate against over-refusal rate together rather than optimizing either one in isolation.
